title_full_ar: المسند الصحيح المختصر من السنن بنقل العدل عن العدل إلى رسول الله ﷺ
subject: hadith
summary: Sahih Muslim is the second most authoritative hadith collection in Sunni Islam, compiled by Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj al-Qushayri al-Naysaburi (204–261 AH / 820–875 CE). Together with Sahih al-Bukhari, it forms al-Sahihayn ('the two Sahihs'), the most trusted corpus of prophetic narrations in the tradition.
overview:
Imam Muslim ibn al-Hajjaj was born in Nishapur (present-day Iran) around 204 AH / 820 CE and died there in 261 AH / 875 CE. He was a student of Imam al-Bukhari and other major hadith scholars of his era, including Yahya ibn Yahya al-Naysaburi, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and Ibn Rahawayh. Like al-Bukhari, he travelled extensively to gather hadith from scholars across the Islamic world.

Muslim's criterion for inclusion differs from al-Bukhari's in one significant respect: he required that two narrators in the chain be contemporaries — that is, that it be possible for them to have met — rather than requiring evidence that they actually met. This makes Muslim's isnads marginally less restrictive in this regard, though many scholars consider his method of organising the text superior to al-Bukhari's for the reader. Muslim himself is reported to have said that he presented his collection to Abu Zur'a al-Razi, one of the greatest hadith critics of the era, who validated it.

The collection reportedly contains around 7,500 hadith with repetitions (approximately 3,033 unique narrations, depending on the counting method), selected from a pool Muslim claimed to have examined of some 300,000 narrations. The structure is organised into chapters (abwab) grouped under major subjects: faith (iman), purity, prayer, zakah, fasting, pilgrimage, marriage, divorce, trade, inheritance, jihad, and more. Uniquely, Muslim provides an important introduction (al-muqaddimah) in which he discusses the principles of hadith criticism, the conditions for authentic transmission, and why he structured the work as he did — making it a valuable methodological text in its own right.

One of Muslim's distinctive contributions is his practice of grouping all the chains (asanid) of a single narration together in one place, rather than distributing them under different chapters. This makes his collection particularly useful for studying the full transmission history of individual hadith and for understanding which wordings of a narration are primary versus variant.

The standard and most celebrated commentary on Sahih Muslim is al-Minhaj by Imam Yahya ibn Sharaf al-Nawawi (d. 676 AH / 1277 CE), also known as Sharh al-Nawawi ala Sahih Muslim. Spanning eighteen volumes in many editions, it explains difficult vocabulary, derives legal rulings, addresses apparent contradictions, and links individual narrations to the broader fiqh discussion across the four madhabs. Al-Nawawi's commentary has remained the primary reference for Sahih Muslim for over seven centuries. Later commentaries include Ikmal al-Mualim by Qadi Iyad (d. 544 AH) and Ikmal Ikmal al-Mualim by al-Ubayy (d. 827 AH).

The most critically edited Arabic text is the Dar Ihya al-Turath al-Arabi edition (Beirut), edited by Muhammad Fuad Abd al-Baqi, which also provides numbering of individual hadith — the standard reference system used by scholars globally. The complete English translation is by Abdul Hamid Siddiqui (published in four volumes by Sh. Muhammad Ashraf, Lahore) and a revised English translation was produced by Nasiruddin al-Khattab (Darussalam, 2007).

The reception of Sahih Muslim among scholars has been uniformly positive, though some classical critics noted a small number of narrations — particularly in the book of faith (Kitab al-Iman) — that they considered open to scrutiny on chains involving certain narrators. Ibn al-Salah (d. 643 AH) in his Muqaddimah and al-Daraqutni (d. 385 AH) in his Ilzamat wa al-Tatabbu' compiled lists of hadith in both Sahihayn that they considered technically deficient; scholars like Ibn Hajar and al-Nawawi responded to these critiques extensively, upholding the overwhelming majority of narrations. The consensus of the ummah has been to accept both Sahihayn as the most authoritative post-Quranic sources. Sahih Muslim is available in full at sunnah.com.
structure: 56 books (kutub), approximately 7,500 hadith with repetitions, approximately 3,033 unique narrations
